tagline.text: The museum of Philippine political history on the Malolos plaza

location.label: Location
location.text: Paseo del Congreso, Plaza Rizal, Malolos City, Bulacan

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0~300 (admission, parking and transport extra, per person)

children.text: Casa Real is a colonial-style building beside Plaza Rizal in Malolos, now run by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) as the Museum of Philippine Political History. It shows relics of the First Republic, Aguinaldo memorabilia and an exhibit on the 21 Women of Malolos, and Barasoain Church and Malolos Cathedral are within walking distance.

Casa Real means "royal house" in Spanish, a name often given to town administration buildings in the Spanish colonial era. Malolos's Casa Real stands on Paseo del Congreso beside Plaza Rizal and now houses the Museum of Philippine Political History (Museo ng Kasaysayang Pampulitika ng Pilipinas), operated by the NHCP. Wikipedia says the building was first built in 1580 and restored in 1852, when it served as a municipal library. It also notes that the present building is a restoration of the original structure, so rather than expecting an untouched original, it is more accurate to think of it as an exhibition hall rebuilt on a historic site.

The building has served many purposes over time. In the Spanish era it was the residence and office of the gobernadorcillo, the highest town official, and visitor accounts say that during the Philippine Revolution it acted as the Imprenta Nacional (national printing press), printing newspapers and documents such as constitutions. After the Philippine–American War it served as the Bulacan provincial capitol until 1930, and a historical marker was installed in 1990. If you know that Malolos was the center of the First Republic (the Malolos Republic) in 1899, you can see how this one building ties into the city's trail of historic sites.

The museum was originally in the NHCP building on Kalaw Avenue beside Rizal Park in Manila, and moved to this Casa Real on October 12, 2016. According to Wikipedia, its exhibits include First Republic relics, memorabilia of General Emilio Aguinaldo, relics left by wealthy Malolos families, a printing press of the Malolos Republic, and a display on the "Women of Malolos". It is not a large museum, and even a slow visit takes around an hour, so rather than coming just for this, combine it with Barasoain Church and Malolos Cathedral for a half-day history route. Labels may mix Filipino and English, so reading a little background beforehand helps a lot. Staff can tell you which relics are most popular and whether photography is allowed.

A few things to know before you go. Opening hours and admission differ between sources. One visitor account says entry is free and parking costs ₱25, and when NHCP museums reopened in 2021 it was reported that they would be open Tuesday to Sunday, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., with free admission. This information is several years old, so please check the NHCP announcements or confirm on site for closing days and fees before visiting.

blocks.title: Permanent exhibit on Philippine political history

children.text: This museum shows how the Philippines' forms of government changed from colonial rule to the founding of a republic. Rather than walking along a big timeline, it suits reading the explanation of each relic one by one. It is the best first stop for understanding the congress and constitution of the Malolos Republic.

Wikipedia lists relics of the First Philippine Republic and the memorabilia of General Emilio Aguinaldo as the main exhibits. Seeing traces of the republic that was launched in Malolos in 1899 in person is the heart of this place.

This exhibit ties in with the story that the building served as a national printing press during the revolution. Remembering that writing and newspapers were tools of the revolution makes a single printing press read more vividly.

This exhibit tells the story of 21 young women of Malolos who confronted the governor-general to demand education for women. They are among the most talked-about figures of this area, so it is a good way to get context before seeing the museum at Barasoain Church. Seeing the related exhibit at the Barasoain museum afterward makes the story far more three-dimensional.
Relics such as furniture and household items left by the city's wealthy families are displayed as well. Beyond politics, it is a pleasure to glimpse how people of Malolos lived in the 19th century.
The building itself revives a colonial-style administrative building, so the exterior makes a good photo. Plaza Rizal across the way honors José Rizal and is a city-center square where locals rest.

blocks.title: A history route you can walk

children.text: According to a visitor, if you park at Malolos Cathedral and walk along the main road for about 2 minutes, you arrive. Barasoain Church is a few minutes away too, so you can park once and cover all three on foot.
Park near Malolos Cathedral or arrive there and see the cathedral exterior first.
Malolos Cathedral
is close by, so it is easy to move on foot.
Walk along the main road to Casa Real. A visitor reports it takes about 2 minutes on foot. Check how to enter and read the notices at the door.
Look around the political history exhibits. The flow works well if you go in this order: First Republic relics, Aguinaldo memorabilia, the printing press, and the 21 Women exhibit. Around
1 hour
is enough.
Rest for a while at Plaza Rizal and look at the buildings around the square.
Have lunch at a nearby restaurant. Bulacan is also known for its snacks and sweets, so add a dessert.
Head to
Barasoain Church
and see the church and its museum. The church is known as the place where the Malolos Congress met in 1898–1899, which connects with your visit to Casa Real.

Casa Real, Barasoain and Malolos Cathedral are all in the town center, so you can park once and walk between them. Opening times differ from site to site, so it is safer to start with whichever is open.
Leave Manila. Travel can take longer depending on traffic, so it is best to set out early to avoid the rush-hour jams.
Arrive in Malolos and see the cathedral and Casa Real.
After lunch, see Barasoain Church and its museum.
If the Hiyas ng Bulacan Museum in the provincial capitol compound is open, stop by to see Bulacan's history and art together. Admission is listed at about ₱20–50, so confirm on site.
Head back to Manila. Plan your schedule with the evening rush-hour traffic in mind.
Malolos, Bulacan lies north of Manila, and the travel time varies greatly with traffic.
Buses and UV Express vans run toward Malolos via NLEX and MacArthur Highway. Terminals include Monumento and Valenzuela, but routes can change, so confirm locally.
Casa Real is beside Plaza Rizal, so after arriving in Malolos, walk toward the cathedral and plaza.
The most reliable way to confirm exact routes and fares is to ask the staff at the terminal.
According to a visitor, it is convenient to park next to Malolos Cathedral and walk about 2 minutes. Parking in front of the museum is difficult because it is on a main road.
With ride-hailing such as Grab, travel time and fare from central Manila to Malolos vary by time of day.
The churches and museums in central Malolos are within walking distance of each other.
When it is hot you can take a tricycle, and it is best to agree on the fare before riding.

It is an indoor museum, so you can visit any time of year, but because you walk between the plaza and the churches, the dry season from November to May is more comfortable. Even in those months the midday sun is strong, so see the museum in the morning first.
During the rainy season from June to October, rain and typhoons can delay travel, and parts of Bulacan can flood. On rainy days, keep it short and focus on the museum, with less time outdoors.

rows: Best for walking; decorations go up on the plaza at year-end in December

Malolos is an easy day trip from Manila, so an overnight stay is not necessary. If you stay longer, you can use hotels in Malolos or lodging in a nearby city. Check locations and reviews on booking sites for your travel dates.

Meals are easy to find at restaurants and street stalls downtown. Bulacan is so famous for its sweets and snacks that it has been nicknamed the land of sweets. After the museum, buying Bulacan-style sweets as souvenirs is a good idea.

Central Malolos is good for walking because the churches, plaza and museums are close together, but it is hot in the daytime. Between stops, take a break with a cold drink at a cafe or snack shop. If you also want to see the Barasoain museum the same day, keep lunch light and leave the afternoon open.
Check opening hours and closing days against NHCP announcements before you visit. Visitor accounts and news reports differ.
Park first at Malolos Cathedral and walk to Casa Real and Barasoain Church for an easy route.
Carry small cash (₱20 and ₱50 bills) for parking and tricycles.
Seeing the 21 Women exhibit and the Barasoain museum on the same day keeps the story connected.
Plan to visit in the morning to avoid direct midday sun.
Check photography rules at the entrance, and do not touch the relics.
If the history is unfamiliar, reading a short piece about the Malolos Republic and the 1898 Barasoain congress beforehand makes the exhibits much easier to follow.
If your visit falls on a Monday, it may be a closing day. NHCP museums were reported to generally be open Tuesday to Sunday, but check the latest announcement.
Opening hours, admission and closing days differ between sources and can change. Before making a long trip, confirm with the NHCP announcements or by phone.
Parking in front of the museum is hard because of the main road. Follow the visitor advice to park by the cathedral.
The present building is described as a restoration, so expecting an original architectural heritage site may disappoint.
Weekends and holidays can bring crowds of group visitors.
During the rainy season, flooded roads and traffic can occur, so leave plenty of time to get back.
Keep valuables on you and watch for pickpockets in crowds.

A church and museum known as the place where the Malolos Congress met. It is a short walk away.

An old town of Bulacan where churches and town streets remain. It makes a good follow-on route from Malolos.
